On this website you can find documentation about software commonly used in bioinformatic data analyses as well as tutorials about various bioinformatic subjects. On this webpage you can find software organized by topic and for each topic you find a list of commonly used software tools.

If you are working at the University of Amsterdam (UvA) Institute for Biodiversity and Ecosystem Dynamics (IBED) and want to know more about what computational resources are available, please also visit the [computational support teams website](https://ibed.uva.nl/facilities/computational-facilities/ibed-computational-support-team/ibed-computational-support-team.html) and our website with more [computation resources](https://computational-resources-uva-ibed-cs-general-20079b9f20f96949e05.gitlab.io/)

Please, be aware that this page is a work in progress and will be slowly updated over time. If you want to add additional information or feel that something is missing feel free to send an email to [n.dombrowski\@uva.nl](mailto:n.dombrowski@uva.nl){.email}.

## Useful tutorials

New to bioinformatics? Start with the bash and HPC tutorial below. It teaches you how to use the command line and how to run analyses on Crunchomics, the UvA computer cluster, and most other tutorials on this page build on it.

Did you just receive sequencing data and want to check it quickly? Then you can start with [A first look at your sequencing data](https://ndombrowski.github.io/sequencing_qc/) instead. It was written for exactly this situation: you can follow it without any command line experience and without doing the bash tutorial first.

### Getting started with bash

-   [Getting started with bash and an HPC](https://ndombrowski.github.io/cli_workshop/): Start here if you have never used the command line. You learn how to set up a terminal and how to organize and inspect sequencing data with bash. Then you copy the data to Crunchomics, install software and run your first jobs there.
-   [Working with tables using AWK](https://ndombrowski.github.io/AWK_tutorial/): AWK is a command line tool for tables. You can use it to pull out columns, keep only the rows that match a pattern, or merge two tables. You need the command line basics first. You can download the example input files [here](https://github.com/ndombrowski/AWK_tutorial/tree/main/1_Inputfiles).
-   [Keeping track of your code with git](https://fkariminejadasl.github.io/ml-notebooks/git/): Git saves a history of the changes to your scripts, so you can go back to an earlier version and share your code with others. This page is a short overview of the most common git commands.

### Storing data on Crunchomics

-   [Using the local scratch on Crunchomics](source/cli/scratch.qmd): Each compute node on Crunchomics has its own fast, temporary storage. This page shows how to use it for jobs that read or write a lot of data. Read it once you are comfortable running jobs on Crunchomics.
-   [Using the IBED Tape Archive](source/cli/ibed_tape.qmd): Crunchomics is not meant for long-term storage. This page shows how to copy raw data and finished results to IBED's tape archive.

### Writing bash scripts

Once you know the basics, these pages help you write scripts that run on many files and stop safely when something goes wrong. They build on each other, so read them in this order:

-   [For-loops in bash](source/core_tools/bash-for-loops.qmd): How can I run the same tool on many files instead of one?
-   [Checking files in bash scripts](source/core_tools/bash-input-validation.qmd): How can my script skip samples that are already done, or stop with a clear message when an input file is missing?
-   [Bash arrays](source/core_tools/bash-arrays.qmd): How can I store a list of file names in one variable, and when do I not need to?
-   [Stopping scripts on errors with `set -euo pipefail`](source/core_tools/bash-pipefail.qmd): Why does AI often add this line to the top of a script, and when does it help or cause problems?

### Using R

-   [R cookbook](https://ndombrowski.github.io/R_cookbook/): Start here if you are new to R. No coding experience is needed. It takes you from installing R and RStudio to reading, changing, plotting and testing your own data. Work through the first chapters in order.
-   [Changing tables with the tidyverse](https://ndombrowski.github.io/Tidyverse_tutorial/): More practice with filtering, sorting, changing and summarizing tables with dplyr, using a data set of penguin measurements.
-   [Making figures with ggplot2](https://ndombrowski.github.io/Ggplot_tutorial/): Build scatter plots, bar plots, boxplots and more, and adjust colors, axes and themes until a figure is ready for a report or paper.

### Bioinformatic workflows

Pick the group that matches your data.

#### For all sequencing data

-   [Downloading data from NCBI](source/core_tools/ncbi.qmd): Download sequencing reads (from the SRA) and genomes from NCBI, for one sample or many at a time.
-   [A first look at your sequencing data](https://ndombrowski.github.io/sequencing_qc/): Check your data soon after you receive it. You count the reads per sample and make quality reports with FastQC, so you can catch problems while they are still easy to fix. You can follow this tutorial without any command line experience.

#### Amplicon data (e.g. 16S rRNA gene)

-   [From sequencing reads to an ASV table with QIIME 2](source/Qiime/3_evelyn_tutorial_notes.qmd): Use a 16S test data set to remove primers, turn reads into amplicon sequence variants (ASVs) with DADA2 or Deblur, assign taxonomy and calculate diversity. Includes a section on running QIIME 2 on Crunchomics.
-   [Analysing an OTU or ASV table in R](source/Qiime/OTU_table_analysis.qmd): Filter, normalize and visualize your table in R, for example with alpha and beta diversity plots, bar plots of the taxa, and tests for taxa that differ between groups.

#### Metagenomes and microbial genomes

These tutorials were first written for workshops at NIOZ. Some use older tool versions or NIOZ file paths, so you may need to adapt the commands for Crunchomics. They also expect you to be comfortable with bash and AWK.

-   [Assembling a metagenome](https://ndombrowski.github.io/Assembly_tutorial/): Check and clean the reads of three small metagenomes, assemble them into contigs with MEGAHIT and metaSPAdes, and compare the assemblies.
-   [Recovering genomes from metagenomes (binning)](https://ndombrowski.github.io/Binning_tutorial/): Sort the contigs from an assembly into metagenome-assembled genomes (MAGs) with several binning tools. Then combine the results with DAS Tool and check genome quality (CheckM) and taxonomy (GTDB-Tk).
-   [Annotating microbial genomes](https://ndombrowski.github.io/Annotation_workflow/): Predict the genes in a set of genomes and find out what they might do, by comparing them against databases such as COG, arCOG, KEGG and Pfam. All results end up in one table.
-   [Building a species tree](https://ndombrowski.github.io/Phylogeny_tutorial/): Learn how phylogenetic trees are built. Then align marker proteins, trim the alignment and build trees with IQ-TREE, for single proteins and for several proteins combined.


## Custom scripts

- [Custom scripts](source/core_tools/custom_scripts.qmd): A list of custom scripts useful for bioinformatic analyses


## Useful databases A-Z

- [arCOG](source/core_tools/arcog.qmd): Archaeal Clusters of Orthologous Genes (arCOGs) database to analyse archaea
- [COG](source/core_tools/cog.qmd): Cluster of Orthologous Genes (COGs) to analyse bacteria
- [dbCAN](source/core_tools/dbcan.qmd): Database to analyse carbohydrate-active enzymes in genomes
- [FeGenie](source/core_tools/fegenie.qmd): Database to identify iron genes and iron operons in genomes
- [HydDB](source/core_tools/hyddb.qmd): Database to identify hydrogenases in genomes
- [KOfam](source/core_tools/kegg_db.qmd): Database to assign KEGG orthologous (KOs) to protein sequences
- [NCBI-nr](source/core_tools/ncbi_nr.qmd): NCBI's non-redundant (nr) protein database to analyse protein sequences
- [Pfam](source/core_tools/pfam_db.qmd): A collection of protein models to analyse protein sequences
- [PGAP database](source/core_tools/pgap_db.qmd): Successor to the TIGRFAM database
- [TIGRFAM](source/core_tools/tigrfam_db.qmd): A collection of manually curated protein families to analyse prokaryotic sequences
